land.text: the Haudenosaunee homeland in upstate New York, the Finger Lakes and the Mohawk valley, which the 1783 Treaty of Paris left to the United States ('no provisions were made for the Iroquois')

successors.note: The Confederacy itself continues (45,000 enrolled in Canada and 81,000 in the United States in 2010, per the page); the mapped polity ends with the 1784 Treaty of Fort Stanwix, after which the lands shrink by sale (Phelps and Gorham 1788, Big Tree 1797, Canandaigua 1794 affirming land east of the Genesee) and many Haudenosaunee settle in Canada (the Haldimand Tract of 950,000 acres, 1784).

capitals.name: Onondaga (the council fire)
capitals.note: The infobox names Onondaga (village) as the capital and lists the Onondaga Nation's sites over time, 'Manlius, New York, from 1640 onward'; the dot is placed at Syracuse, beside the Onondaga valley, because the pages give no coordinates.

keyframe_review.note: 1450-1571, 72,218 km2. Infobox 'Between 1450 and 1660 (estimate)'; 'Many archaeologists and anthropologists believe that the League was formed about 1450'; 'based in what is now central and west New York State'; 'From east to west, the League was composed of the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, and Seneca nations'. The page gives no area; the gazetteer's Iroquoia region (67,271 km2) is within 7% of the shape.

1572-1639, the same 72,218 km2 as 1450 (no cell differs). No page dates a change in 1572; the break is Cliopatria's split of the row (seed Seshat ids us_haudenosaunee_1 and _2). The shape holds until 1639.

1640-1641, 77,732 km2: the step adds 22 cells (5,564 km2) across the Genesee and Finger Lakes country (lon -78.84 to -76.22), which fits 'They forced the Wenro to disperse in 1638'. The page names the people, not the land.

1642-1652, 78,349 km2: two cells swap at the edges. 1642 is when 'the Haudenosaunee launched their first direct attacks' on Ville-Marie. The Wendat (1648-49), Petun (1650) and Neutral (1651) conquests fall inside this span but the shape does not carry them; the ledger events of 1648-1651 do, up to the 1653 shape.

1653-1658, 122,575 km2: the step adds 170 cells (42,993 km2) across southern Ontario from Huronia to the Niagara and Lake Erie shore (lon -83.07 to -76.22, lat 42.11 to 45.08), matching the Wendat (1649), Petun (1650), Neutral (1651) and Erie ('destroyed the Erie confederacy by 1656'; the Iroquois page says 1657) conquests. The shape anticipates the Erie by three years.

1659-1669, 286,791 km2: the step adds 657 cells (166,155 km2) between Lake Erie and the Ohio River (lon -84.97 to -77.35, lat 38.48 to 42.5). The one page that dates the Ohio country says the Ohio River watershed became hunting ground 'from about 1670', so this step may run up to eleven years ahead of the page; kept because the Erie were destroyed by 1656 and the page says conquest left 'the Ohio Valley, southern Michigan, and southern Ontario depopulated'. Low confidence in the 1659 start.

1670-1672, 447,297 km2: the step adds 616 cells (155,786 km2) west to Lake Michigan and north to 46.01 N. 'Ohio River watershed became Haudenosaunee hunting grounds from about 1670'. A claim and a hunting ground, not settled territory; the page also says the Michigan peninsula was emptied by the wars.

1673-1676, 469,833 km2: the step adds 96 cells (24,278 km2) in West Virginia and the Virginia Piedmont edge (lat 38.05 to 39.61). The page dates the driving of the Mannahoac from the northern Virginia Piedmont to 1670, three years earlier.

1677-1682, 544,196 km2: the step adds 299 cells (75,617 km2) in central and eastern Pennsylvania (lon -78.55 to -74.86, lat 39.05 to 42.39), which is the Susquehannock country. 'Susquehannock moved south into Maryland' in 1675 and 'The survivors of the siege were eventually absorbed by the Iroquois'; the Iroquois page says the Susquehannock were defeated in 1680.

1683-1686, 570,382 km2 (the maximum): unverified, page silent. The step adds 119 cells (30,095 km2) scattered over Ohio, Michigan and Ontario (lat 37.99 to 45.68). The page mentions only La Salle's 1681 treaty with the Miami and Illinois and a 1684 council (Covenant Chain page); no acquisition is dated.

1687-1701, 533,135 km2: 148 cells (37,429 km2) drop out around the outer edges of the claim. 'In June 1687, Governor Denonville and Pierre de Troyes set out' for Fort Frontenac; and the page calls the Iroquois' Ohio and Illinois control 'brief' and says it 'was lost' after 1689 (an Anishinaabeg ambush near South Bend in 1689 destroyed most of an Iroquois raiding party). The shape is kept to 1701 as the claim: the Nanfan deed of 1701 names the same hunting ground 'by right of conquest'.

1702-1717, 75,283 km2: the claim of 451,932 km2 is gone and only the homeland (Iroquoia) remains. 19 July 1701: the Nanfan deed of the beaver hunting grounds to the English; 4 August 1701: the Great Peace of Montreal, where 'The Haudenosaunee promised to be neutral in case of conflict between the French and English colonies'.

1718-1726, identical to 1702 (no cell differs). Inside the span: 'In about 1722, the Iroquoian-speaking Tuscarora joined the League' (sixth nation) and the 14 September 1726 amendment of the Nanfan deed. The shape draws neither the Tuscarora tract (no page names one) nor the 1726 reserved strip.

1727-1733, 75,024 km2: three cells change near the Genesee and Oswego (lat 43.3 to 43.4), 0.3%. The 1726 amendment reserved 'a strip of land 60 miles wide adjoining Lakes Erie and Ontario, starting at Sandusky Creek' for Six Nations use; the shape (west edge -78.68) does not draw it, and the ledger's 1726 event is a caption only.

1734-1740, 72,363 km2: nine cells (2,276 km2) on the west shore of Lake Champlain (lon -73.8 to -73.36, lat 44.03 to 45.11) leave the shape; all nine lie inside Cliopatria's New France shape of 1734. No page opened dates it.
1741-1756, 71,567 km2: two cells (0.7%) on the Champlain shore; below the level the pages can explain. No event.

1757-1761, 67,750 km2: 16 cells (4,046 km2) are lost along the northern and eastern edge (lat 43.21 to 45.23), 13 of them inside Cliopatria's British Colonial Empire shape. The Iroquois page: 'During the French and Indian War, the Iroquois briefly fought on both sides while trying to maintain neutrality'; no land named.
1762, 67,186 km2: three cells gained, four lost (under 1%). No event.

1763-1768, 43,334 km2: 97 cells (24,531 km2) are lost round the heartland's rim (lon -78.6 to -73.83, lat 41.91 to 45.25), 96 of them inside Cliopatria's British Colonial Empire shape. The Iroquois page: 'the British government issued the Royal Proclamation of 1763, forbidding white settlement beyond the Appalachian Mountains', which does not touch New York; the page is silent on this contraction.

1769-1774, 15,108 km2: 101 cells (25,543 km2) more are lost (lon -78.51 to -73.81, lat 42.23 to 45.23), 93 of them inside the British Colonial Empire shape; what is left is the Finger Lakes and Oneida core. The 5 November 1768 treaty page names Kentucky, West Virginia and the Pennsylvania 'New Purchase', not New York, so the page does not explain this contraction.
1775, 14,565 km2: four cells (1,012 km2) at lat 42.39 to 43.34 drop out for one year and return in 1776; a Cliopatria artefact with no page behind it. No event.

1776-1777, 15,108 km2: back to the 1769 shape. 'During the American Revolution, the League broke down. The Oneida and Tuscarora supported the colonists, while the rest of the Iroquois League (the Cayuga, Mohawk, Onondaga, and Seneca) sided with the British and Loyalists.'

1778-1780, 15,156 km2. The Sullivan Expedition (18 June to 3 October 1779) razed about 40 villages of the Seneca and Cayuga in the Finger Lakes and 'drove just over 5,000 Haudenosaunee to Fort Niagara'; the shape does not change in 1779, so the ledger carries it as a short contest.

1781-1782 in Cliopatria, 15,156 km2; the years are extended to 1784 (October) because the Confederacy still held its homeland after the 1783 Treaty of Paris, which 'ignored' its lands, until the 22 October 1784 Treaty of Fort Stanwix.

correction.text: the Finger Lakes and Oneida core, unchanged; only the years change, 1781 to 1784 (the treaty of 22 October 1784)

region.text: central and west New York State, from the Mohawk in the east to the Seneca in the west

ledger.note: c. 1450: the Five Nations League of the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca is formed under the Great Law of Peace. 'Many archaeologists and anthropologists believe that the League was formed about 1450'; infobox 'Between 1450 and 1660 (estimate)', text 'likely formed between 1142 and 1660' with 'little widespread consensus'. The year is Cliopatria's and the one the page prefers.

region.text: the Wenro country west of the Seneca, across the Genesee and Finger Lakes, the 22 cells the 1640 shape adds

ledger.note: 1638: the Wenro are dispersed. 'They forced the Wenro to disperse in 1638.' The page names the people, not the land; Cliopatria's shape grows in 1640.

region.text: Huronia, the Wendat country between Georgian Bay and Lake Simcoe (the pages name the people; the discs are the researcher's reading)

ledger.note: 1648: the Haudenosaunee strike the Wendat. 'launched a devastating attack into the heart of Wendat territory' (winter, with Jesuit missionaries killed and thousands taken captive); the Iroquois page dates the Huron defeat to 1649.

region.text: Huronia, the Wendat country between Georgian Bay and Lake Simcoe (the pages name the people; the discs are the researcher's reading)

ledger.note: 16 March 1649: the Haudenosaunee enter Wendake. 'a Haudenosaunee war party of about 1,000 entered Wendake and burned the Huron mission villages' (Huron people page: 'March 16, 1649'). Mirror of the wendat-confederacy occupation_start; added by the am-05 reviewer.

region.text: Huronia, the Wendat country between Georgian Bay and Lake Simcoe (the pages name the people; the discs are the researcher's reading)

ledger.note: May 1649: the occupation ends in annexation (the gain below). 'By May 1, 1649, the Huron had burned 15 of their villages' and about 10,000 'fled to Gahoendoe'. Mirror of the wendat-confederacy occupation_end; added by the am-05 reviewer.

region.text: Huronia, the Wendat country between Georgian Bay and Lake Simcoe (the pages name the people; the discs are the researcher's reading)

ledger.note: 1649: Huronia falls. The Iroquois page: 'they defeated and assimilated most of the Huron (1649)'; the survivors flee, and a 1656 raid on the Ile d'Orleans drives the remnant into Quebec (Beaver Wars page). Month from the Huron people page: 'By May 1, 1649, the Huron had burned 15 of their villages' and fled to Gahoendoe.

region.text: Huronia, the Wendat country between Georgian Bay and Lake Simcoe (the pages name the people; the discs are the researcher's reading)

ledger.note: 1649: the Haudenosaunee take Huronia. 'defeated and assimilated most of the Huron (1649)'. The page gives the year and the people; the land is the researcher's reading. Month from the Huron people page: 'By May 1, 1649, the Huron had burned 15 of their villages' and fled to Gahoendoe.

region.text: the Petun (Tionontati) country south of Nottawasaga Bay (the pages name the people, not the land)

ledger.note: 1650: the Petun are defeated and assimilated ('Petun (1650)').

region.text: the Neutral country of the Niagara peninsula and the Grand River (the pages name the people, not the land)

ledger.note: 1650: the Haudenosaunee attack the Neutral Nation ('1650-1651 attacks on the Neutrals').

region.text: the Neutral country of the Niagara peninsula and the Grand River (the pages name the people, not the land)

ledger.note: 1651: the Neutrals are gone. 'they completely drove the tribe from traditional territory by the end of 1651'; the Iroquois page: 'the Neutral Nation (1651)'.

region.text: the Neutral country of the Niagara peninsula and the Grand River (the pages name the people, not the land)

ledger.note: 1651: the Haudenosaunee take the Neutral country. 'completely drove the tribe from traditional territory by the end of 1651'. The page does not say where that was; Cliopatria's 1653 shape adds the Niagara and Lake Erie shore.

region.text: the Erie country on the south shore of Lake Erie (the pages name the people, not the land)

ledger.note: 1654: the war on the Erie begins ('1654-1656 war against the Erie').

region.text: the Erie country on the south shore of Lake Erie (the pages name the people, not the land)

ledger.note: 1656: the Erie confederacy is destroyed. 'the Iroquois destroyed the Erie confederacy by 1656'; the Iroquois page says the Erie fell in 1657.

region.text: the Erie country on the south shore of Lake Erie (the pages name the people, not the land)

ledger.note: 1656: the Haudenosaunee take the Erie shore of Lake Erie ('destroyed the Erie confederacy by 1656'; 1657 on the Iroquois page).

region.text: the country between Lake Erie and the Ohio River, the 657 cells the 1659 shape adds

ledger.note: 1659: the Ohio country passes to the Haudenosaunee on Cliopatria's shape. Page silent on 1659: the Beaver Wars page dates the Ohio River watershed as hunting ground 'from about 1670' and says the wars left 'the Ohio Valley, southern Michigan, and southern Ontario depopulated'.

region.text: the Susquehannock country of the Susquehanna valley (the pages name the people, not the land)

ledger.note: 1663: the Haudenosaunee besiege the Susquehannock. The Susquehannock 'easily withstood a siege by 800 Seneca, Cayuga and Onondaga in May 1663'; an earlier Mohawk attack in the winter of 1652 was repulsed, and a Susquehannock force destroyed an Onondaga war party in 1666.

region.text: the Ohio River watershed and the Michigan peninsula to Lake Michigan, the 616 cells the 1670 shape adds

ledger.note: c. 1670: the Ohio hunting grounds. 'Ohio River watershed became Haudenosaunee hunting grounds from about 1670'; the Nanfan page says the claim reached 'as far west as Quadoge (now Chicago)'. A claim, not settlement: the wars left it depopulated.

region.text: the northern Virginia Piedmont, from which the Mannahoac were driven (the shape's edge reaches 38.05 N in 1673)

ledger.note: 1670: the Mannahoac are driven from the northern Virginia Piedmont ('Mannahoac driven from the northern Virginia Piedmont'). Cliopatria's shape reaches this country in 1673. The page goes on: 'they claimed the land by right of conquest as a hunting ground. The English acknowledged this claim in 1674 and again in 1684' (this claim is the Mannahoac Piedmont, not the Ohio watershed).

region.text: the Susquehannock country of the Susquehanna valley (the pages name the people, not the land)

ledger.note: 1675: the Susquehannock war ends. 'Susquehannock moved south into Maryland' and were besieged by militias; 'The survivors of the siege were eventually absorbed by the Iroquois'. The Iroquois page dates the defeat of the Susquehannock to 1680.

region.text: central and eastern Pennsylvania, the 299 cells the 1677 shape adds, the Susquehannock country

ledger.note: 1675: the Susquehannock land passes to the Haudenosaunee. 'The survivors of the siege were eventually absorbed by the Iroquois'; Maryland had made peace with the Iroquois in 1674 and dropped the Susquehannock alliance. Cliopatria's shape grows in 1677; the Iroquois page says 1680.

region.text: scattered cells across Ohio, Michigan and Ontario, the 119 cells the 1683 shape adds

ledger.note: 1683: the claim reaches its largest, 570,382 km2. Page silent: the Covenant Chain page has only a 1684 council at which Governor Effingham used the phrase 'covenant chain', and the Beaver Wars page a 1681 French treaty with the Miami and Illinois.

region.text: scattered cells on the outer edge of the claim, the 148 cells the 1687 shape drops

ledger.note: 1687: the claim thins at its edges. Page silent on land: 'In June 1687, Governor Denonville and Pierre de Troyes set out' against the Iroquois, and the Iroquois' Ohio and Illinois control, called 'brief', 'was lost' after the 1689 ambush near South Bend; the shape keeps the claim to 1701.

region.text: the beaver hunting grounds 'as far west as Quadoge (now Chicago)', over parts of the present Midwest and southern Ontario

ledger.note: 1701: the hunting grounds are deeded to the English Crown. 19 July 1701, Albany: the Haudenosaunee grant 'the title to a vast area of land' claimed 'as a hunting ground'; the French did not recognize the deed. 4 August 1701: the Great Peace of Montreal, where 'The Haudenosaunee promised to be neutral in case of conflict between the French and English colonies'.
1722: the Five Nations become the Six Nations ('They have also been called the Six Nations (Five Nations before 1722)').

region.text: the Tuscarora took their place within the Confederacy under Oneida sponsorship; the pages name no tract

ledger.note: 1722: the Tuscarora join as the sixth nation. 'In 1722, sponsored by the Oneida, the Tuscarora were accepted as the sixth nation of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy'; the Iroquois page: 'In about 1722'. Only part of the Tuscarora came north.

region.text: nine cells on the west shore of Lake Champlain

ledger.note: 1734: the Champlain shore leaves the shape. Page silent; all nine cells lie inside Cliopatria's New France shape of 1734.

region.text: 16 cells along the northern and eastern edge of the heartland

ledger.note: 1757: the heartland's northern and eastern edge thins. Page silent; 13 of the 16 cells lie inside Cliopatria's British Colonial Empire shape.

region.text: 97 cells round the rim of the heartland (24,531 km2)

ledger.note: 1763: the rim of the Iroquois country passes to the British colonies on Cliopatria's shape. Page silent: the Royal Proclamation of 1763 'forbidding white settlement beyond the Appalachian Mountains' concerns the west; 96 of the 97 cells lie inside Cliopatria's British Colonial Empire shape.

region.text: 'the Kentucky portion of the Virginia Colony' and most of present-day West Virginia, the line following the Ohio River as far as the Tennessee River

ledger.note: 1768: the Ohio hunting ground is ceded. 5 November 1768, Fort Stanwix: the Six Nations, who 'claimed ownership by conquest over land as far south as the Tennessee River', cede the land to the Crown. The Shawnee and Lenape were present but 'were not signatories'. The keyframes have drawn none of this land since 1702, so no cells change.

region.text: 101 cells round the rim of the heartland (25,543 km2), leaving the Finger Lakes and Oneida core

ledger.note: 1769: the heartland shrinks to its core on Cliopatria's shape. Page silent: the 1768 treaty page names no New York land; 93 of the 101 cells lie inside Cliopatria's British Colonial Empire shape.

region.text: the Finger Lakes towns of the Seneca and Cayuga, razed in the Sullivan Expedition

ledger.note: 1779: the Sullivan Expedition marches into Iroquoia. 'on June 18 when the army marched from Easton, Pennsylvania'; led by John Sullivan and James Clinton.

region.text: the Finger Lakes towns of the Seneca and Cayuga

ledger.note: 1779: the expedition ends on 3 October with about 40 Haudenosaunee villages razed and 'just over 5,000 Haudenosaunee' driven to Fort Niagara; it 'depopulated the area for post-war settlement'. Counter-raids follow in 1780 (Harpersfield in April, Caughnawaga in May, the Schoharie and Mohawk valleys in October).

region.text: claims to the Ohio territory, 'a strip of land along the east side of the Niagara River', and 'all land west of mouth of Buffalo creek'

ledger.note: 1784: the Six Nations cede their claims at Fort Stanwix. 22 October 1784: 'gave up claims to the Ohio territory, a strip along the Niagara River, and all land west of mouth of Buffalo creek'; the council at Buffalo Creek refused to ratify, and the Shawnee, Seneca-Cayuga and Lenape rejected the treaty.

region.text: the Haudenosaunee homeland in upstate New York

ledger.note: 1784: the Confederacy's territory passes under the United States. The Iroquois page: 'At the war's conclusion with the 1783 Treaty of Paris, no provisions were made for the Iroquois'; 'Another Treaty of Fort Stanwix was signed with the U.S. in 1784'; 'followed by another treaty in 1794 at Canandaigua'. The Confederacy lives on, in New York and on the Haldimand Tract of 950,000 acres in Ontario granted in 1784 (Sullivan Expedition page), but no shape is drawn after 1784.

wars.name: Mohawk-Mahican War

zones.text: Fort Orange and the upper Hudson, where the Mohawk gained direct access to Dutch trade

wars.outcome: The Mohawks defeated the Mahicans and secured direct access to Dutch trade at Fort Orange.
wars.note: The page gives 1624-1628 for the war; the land is inside the Mohawk's eastern frontier and moves no Cliopatria border.

wars.name: Beaver Wars

zones.text: Huronia, the Wendat country between Georgian Bay and Lake Simcoe (the pages name the people; the discs are the researcher's reading)
the Neutral country of the Niagara peninsula and the Grand River (the pages name the people, not the land)
the Erie country on the south shore of Lake Erie (the pages name the people, not the land)
the Susquehannock country of the Susquehanna valley (the pages name the people, not the land)
the Ohio River watershed, claimed by conquest as hunting ground from about 1670

wars.outcome: The Haudenosaunee destroyed the Wendat (1649), Petun (1650), Neutral (1651) and Erie (1656) and absorbed the Susquehannock (1675), claiming the Ohio country; French and Anishinaabe resistance from 1687 ended the conquests, and the Great Peace of Montreal (4 August 1701) and the Nanfan deed (19 July 1701) closed the wars.
wars.note: The Iroquois page dates the Erie to 1657 and the Susquehannock to 1680; the war spans 'Beginning in 1609' (Champlain and the Algonquin against the Haudenosaunee, summer 1609) to 1701. Raids on the French (Ville-Marie 1642, Trois-Rivieres 1653, Lachine 4 August 1689, La Prairie 1691) and French expeditions (Tracy 1666, Denonville 1687, 1692) took no ground, so no French contest is recorded.

wars.name: Sullivan Expedition

zones.text: the Finger Lakes, Genesee and Chemung country, 'the heartland of Upstate New York'

wars.outcome: About 40 Haudenosaunee villages razed and over 5,000 refugees driven to Fort Niagara; the area depopulated 'for post-war settlement'.
wars.note: 18 June to 3 October 1779; Sullivan and Clinton. The only major battle was at Newtown on the Chemung River (29 August, narrated without the name).

wars.name: Loyalist and Haudenosaunee raids on the Mohawk and Schoharie valleys
wars.outcome: Brant's raid on Harpersfield (April), the destruction of Caughnawaga (May) and Sir John Johnson's burning of 200 dwellings (October); no change of border.
wars.note: Retaliation for the 1779 expedition; 59 war parties left Fort Niagara between February and September 1780 (Butler).

certainty.note: Throughout the borders are approximate: the pages give peoples, hunting-ground claims and treaty lines in miles, not surveyed frontiers. The Fort Stanwix lines of 1768 and 1784 are treaty lines but run outside the Cliopatria heartland.

notes: Nine pages opened (budget up to 9 for 24 shapes). The Haudenosaunee Confederacy is alive today (45,000 enrolled in Canada and 81,000 in the United States in 2010, per the Iroquois page); end is set to the 1784 Treaty of Fort Stanwix because Cliopatria draws no shape after 1782 and the pages describe the homeland passing under the United States (Paris 1783, Fort Stanwix 1784); the Cliopatria 1781 shape is extended to 1784 for that reason. Honest limits: (1) the Ohio/Michigan/Illinois 'territory' of 1659-1701 (up to 570,382 km2) is a hunting-ground claim by conquest, left depopulated by the wars (Beaver Wars page); the renderer may want it lighter than the homeland, and the Nanfan deed of 1701 and the 1768 cession name the same land; no page calls any people a vassal of the Haudenosaunee, so no vassal events are recorded (rule 4); (2) from 1683 to 1687 the shapes' growth and from 1734 to 1769 the contraction of the rim are not explained by any page opened (events at confidence 1 with the counterpart read from which Cliopatria shape covers the lost cells); (3) the 1726 strip on Lakes Erie and Ontario and the 1768 Kentucky and West Virginia cession name land the Cliopatria shapes never draw since 1702: they are captions, not cell changes; (4) the French contest is not recorded because the pages show raids and expeditions, not ground held (Lachine, La Prairie, Trois-Rivieres, Denonville 1687, 1692); (5) cell changes below 1% of the area (1718, 1741, 1762, 1775, 1776) carry no event; (6) the Great Peace of Montreal of 4 August 1701 has no ledger event of its own (no type fits a treaty with no territorial term) and sits in the Nanfan loss caption and the Beaver Wars entry; (7) the French and Indian War and the American Revolution are not given as war entries because no page opened dates their start; the Sullivan Expedition and the 1780 raids are. Dates the pages dispute: Erie 1656 (Beaver Wars) or 1657 (Iroquois); Huron 1648 winter raid (Beaver Wars) or 1649 (Iroquois); Susquehannock 1675 or 1680. The Haldimand Tract (950,000 acres, 1784, Sullivan page) and the Six Nations of the Grand River have no land named on the pages: a gap-filler should open 'Haldimand Proclamation' and 'Six Nations of the Grand River'. Counterparts needing dossiers: wendat-confederacy (this group, written after this one), the Neutral Nation, Erie, Susquehannock, Petun, Wenro, Mannahoac, Mahican and Tuscarora (small peoples; no Cliopatria row); united-states-of-america, new-france and english/british colonial empires belong to am-07/am-06/eu-11 and should carry the mirror events (the 1701 gain by the English, the 1768 and 1784 gains by the Crown and the United States). Gazetteer: all names used resolve (Iroquoia, Ohio Country, places Orillia, Barrie, Hamilton, Cleveland, Erie, Harrisburg, Williamsport, Buffalo, Albany, rivers Niagara and Mohawk); the Petun, Mannahoac and Wenro lands are expressed as discs because the gazetteer lacks Huronia, Petun, Neutral and Erie country regions.
